Why is this in /v/Conspiracy?

Cloud seeding is neither new nor secretive.

I'm more used to seeing articles ridicule weather modification, under the impression that weather modification is a subject of tinfoil hats and only nutters believe it is currently being carried out in our skies. At least, that's the impression i get when discussing it most places. The conspiracy is in the denial of operations like these, and the fact that if governments are willing to pump large sums of money (like this case) into operations like this, then why is it "ridiculous" that they are not spraying silver iodide pellets from the back of planes for the process of cloud seeding?

Isn't the ridicule mainly based on the low amount of evidence suggesting that these tactics actually do anything, not the fact that governments are openly executing these practices? Cloud seeding was a hot topic of news even back in 2008. If someone is actively denying the existence of cloud seeding with how open it already is, I doubt they're worth trying to convince.

We've been cloud seeding since the 60's or so. Definitely by the 70's. If there was ever a land war with Russia the US planned to heavily seed clouds to monsoon conditions. Turning everything to mud and bogging down or hampering Russian troop movements and particularly tank columns.

Here's the key points of the article. I realize i misspelled "Chinese" in the title, but can't seem to edit it, sorry about that.

Run by the Weather Modification Department, a division of the Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences, the program employs and trains 32,000 to 35,000 people across China, some of them farmers, who are paid to handle anti-aircraft guns and rocket launchers [source: Aiyar]. These heavy-duty weapons launch pellets containin­g silver iodide into clouds. Silver iodide is thought to concentrate moisture and cause rain, a process known as cloud seeding. China has invested heavily in this technology, using more than 12,000 anti-aircraft guns and rocket launchers in addition to about 30 planes [source: Aiyar].

The Beijing Weather Modification Office spent a lot of time researching how to prevent rain in the city during the Aug. 8 opening ceremony of the 2008 Summer Olympics. The government even guaranteed clear skies for the event -- a promise it managed to deliver on. The feat only took the launch of 1,104 rain dispersal rockets from 21 sites in the city to pull off [source: O'Neill].

Even in areas with very low humidity, there's at least some water in the sky and clouds. A rainstorm happens after moisture collects around naturally occurring particles in the air, causing the air to reach a level of saturation at which point it can no longer hold in that moisture. Cloud seeding essentially helps that process along, providing additional "nuclei" around which water condenses. These nuclei can be salts, calcium chloride, dry ice or silver iodide, which the Chinese use. Silver iodide is effective because its form is similar to ice crystals. Calcium chloride is often used in warm or tropical areas.

Scientists may not be sure if cloud seeding actually works, but despite the skepticism, China is moving forward. The nation spends $60 to $90 million a year on weather modification, in addition to the $266 million spent from 1995 to 2003 [source: Things Asian]. The government plans to produce 1.7 trillion cubic feet (50 billion cubic meters) of rain a year through the practice [source: Aiyar].

Hello,

I am very enthusiastic about voat and I don't want it to become reddit v2.0. For that not to happen, we need to think outside the box, not be bound by what reddit does and doesn't and learn from the mistakes of others.

I have sketched in my mind a vision of what Voat should be. Not all of these ideas are mine, I link to posts where I got them. These are pretty radical ideas, so I'll need you to clear your mind of what we have now, bear with me and think about it. Then tell me why it sucks or not.

There are 3 big shifts of paradigm that I would love to see. I will list pros/cons tables at the end of the post detailing why each would be a good idea and some cons/problems to solve. I will keep updating them with more pros and cons as you keep commenting on the ideas.

1. No user karma.

The premise is to keep counting upvoats and downvoats on posts and comments, but not to count user score.

This has been discussed in some threads.

Pros Cons
Discourages karma whoring and reputation (positive or negative) farming. People with a long history of quality comments and posts would have no way of showing it.*)
Encourages sharing of things you're actually passionate about and want people to see, as opposed to being rewarded for mechanical reposting. ?
People aren't punished for going against the hivemind -- downvoat brigading of users' previous posts/comments is pointless. ?

*) Then again, people who are passionate about something and post a lot of quality content about it probably don't expect or need any sort of reward in the first place.

2. Subreddits as tags.

This is not as drastic of a change (from the user's perspective) and I think it could bring lots of flexibility to the site. The idea is that subverses would be treated similarly to hashtags. When submitting a post, you could choose a multitude of subverses that you deem relevant to the post and you could then have a limited ability to change the post's subverse list. It would then show up to users subscribed to one or more of these subverses.

Proposed here.

Pros Cons
Increases post flexibility and eliminates the need to completely delete posts that are off-topic in a certain subverse (it would suffice to delete the tag). Subverses to which the post has been submited couldn't be visible in the URL.
Eliminates the need for x-posts and users subscribed to both subverses don't need to see the same post twice. Would probably require a massive rework of code.
Greatly eases the discovery of new niche, but potentially interesting subverses. People might try to spam every subverse that seems half-relevant. (point raised by @casebash)

3. Upvoats and downvoats as agree/disagree buttons.

People keep telling everyone to use upvoats and downvoats as "contributes to discussion" and "doesn't contribute to discussion" buttons. Everyone doesn't care and use them as agree and disagree buttons anyway, because that's the first natural thing to use them as. Why not embrace this and actually use them as agree/disagree buttons? You could then have downvoats contribute positively to the post/comment's visibility. Of course, with this system in place, we'd need a way to mark posts and comments as junk -- but we already have that: the Report Spam button. It could double as a "mark comment as junk" thing, contributing negatively to its visibility.

Discussed here.

Pros Cons
Votes are used for the purpose for which it feels natural to use them. Downvoat brigading to silence a user might change to "mark as junk" brigading. How to solve?
Posts going against the hivemind are not silenced. Controversial posts (that however do contribute to discussion) are automatically ranked high. ?
Junk posts are marked as such and can be safely ignored by users. ?
Controversial content is not buried if a few first downvoters disagree. Discussion about controversial ideas is promoted, not discouraged. ?
My vision of Voat: No user karma, subverses as tags and votes as agree/disagree buttons. Please give me reasons why it would or wouldn't work.
Regarding 3: Does it really matter what its called? Though personally I'm more likely to upvoat something I disagree with that makes a compelling case than I am something I reflexively agree with.

It doesn't matter what it's called. The important thing is the shift of thinking.

You may do that and lots of voaters may do that, but if this platform ever becomes popular, I feel like it's safe to presume that the majority of users wouldn't.

There's another massive con for 2. If a subverse was like a tag, then people would most likely spam every subverse that seemed half-relevant, without regard to the scope defined in the sidebar. If someone is going to be posting the same content in multiple subs, I want them to have made that decision manually. This leads to more of the content in a sub to be posted by the regulars of a sub, not by someone who has never heard of the sub before and has no idea of what kind of content the users are interested in.

Instead of 3, I would prefer an option to disable downvotes. Like an actual option, not just a CSS hack like Reddit uses. Each sub should be able to decide for itself whether downvotes are useful or not.

Good point about #2.

IMO the option to disable downvotes doesn't really do anything though. The main change proposed in #3 would be that the contribution of downvotes would be positive towards a post's visibility. If downvotes were disabled, nothing would change -- just "I'll downvote this" to "I won't upvote this".

"IMO the option to disable downvotes doesn't really do anything though" - well, controversial posts would be much less likely to be buried than under the status quo. There are subs, like politics, where this is really important. For other subs, this is much less important.

Personally, I liked the idea behind 2, but the issues that you brought up dashed my liking of it. It could work if you limited it to 2-3 tags at once, but that would require a lot of work to implement and would be a mostly unnecessary change.

Official crossposting functions (with a similar 2-3 sub limit) would be good though and presumably much easier to implement. It would need to contain a reminder to read the rules of each subverse you're posting to and to respect the community's wishes. It even could cut down on spam by only putting the first subverse chosen on all instead of each of them, allowing people to crosspost with it looking like spam on /v/all.

Instead of 3, I would prefer an option to disable downvotes. Like an actual option, not just a CSS hack like Reddit uses. Each sub should be able to decide for itself whether downvotes are useful or not.
